meta.title: Who really said "Well, nobody's perfect"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: The line is real and correctly quoted. Billy Wilder and I. A. L. Diamond wrote it for Some Like It Hot (1959); Joe E. Brown only spoke it.
meta.ogDescription: Correctly quoted — but the authors are Billy Wilder and I. A. L. Diamond, not the actor Joe E. Brown. Some Like It Hot (1959), AFI's No. 48.

answer.sourceLine: It is the closing line of Some Like It Hot (1959), written by Billy Wilder and I. A. L. Diamond and spoken on screen by Osgood Fielding III. The popular wording is the real wording — Wikiquote’s transcription of the closing exchange ↗ reads “Well, nobody’s perfect!” and AFI prints the same sentence at No. 48 ↗. What usually goes wrong is the credit, not the words.

source.excerpt: Daphne/Jerry [whips off his wig, and changes to a manly voice]: “Uhhh, I’m a man!” — Osgood [looks at him then turns back, unperturbed]: “Well, nobody’s perfect!”
trail: The wording. Wikiquote’s transcription of the film’s dialogue ↗ gives the final exchange in full and ends on the bolded line “Well, nobody’s perfect!” The popular wording and the transcribed wording are the same sentence.

The authorship, from the body that ranked it. The American Film Institute’s own list ↗ carries the line at No. 48 and names the writers as Billy Wilder and I. A. L. Diamond; the tabulated list detail ↗ adds the speaker and performer, Osgood Fielding III and Joe E. Brown.

Whether the film borrowed it. The film’s production history ↗ shows an adaptation of an earlier screenplay — Fanfare of Love (1935), by way of its 1951 German remake — but records that Wilder built the gangster plot, and it names no novel or play behind the closing scene. The same page reports that the line went into the script as a placeholder.

Whether the words were new. They were not. Page 58 of the 1872 second volume of Middlemarch ↗ has Caleb Garth say “Well, well, nobody’s perfect, but”. No claim of influence is made here — only that the film cannot be credited with the phrase itself.
source.excerptNote: The exchange is the end of a run of escalating confessions — not a natural blonde, a smoker, a terrible past, no children — each of which Osgood waves away. Sources differ on one mark of punctuation and nothing else: Wikiquote’s transcription ends on an exclamation mark ↗, while AFI prints a period ↗. The words are identical.

source.rightsNote: Some Like It Hot was released on March 19, 1959 by United Artists for The Mirisch Company ↗ — far too late for the United States public domain, which reaches published works through 1930. Screen writing is work for hire, so the copyright in the dialogue sits with the studio and its successors rather than with Wilder or Diamond or their estates; quoting the closing line for identification and commentary, as here, is a different matter from reproducing the screenplay. The 1872 Middlemarch passage quoted elsewhere on this page is public domain, but that is a separate work and carries no rights in this line.

author.name: Billy Wilder & I. A. L. Diamond
author.heading: The writers
author.metaLine: Billy Wilder 1906–2002 · I. A. L. Diamond 1920–1988 · screenwriting partners
author.bio: Billy Wilder (June 22, 1906 – March 27, 2002) was an Austrian-American director and screenwriter whose Hollywood career ran across five decades and brought him seven Academy Awards from twenty-one nominations. I. A. L. Diamond (June 27, 1920 – April 21, 1988) was a Romanian-American screenwriter best known for his collaborations with Wilder ↗, of which Some Like It Hot was the first great success. The two shared the screenplay credit and shared the Academy Award nomination for it, which is why this page credits a partnership rather than a name.

misattribution.heading: The words are right. The credit usually isn't.
misattribution.intro: This is an unusual case for a quote page: nothing needs correcting about the sentence. Four plain words in a plain order have survived intact for decades. Everything that goes wrong with this quote happens in the byline.

items.why: Brown delivers the line, and delivery is most of why it works. But AFI credits the writing of entry No. 48 to “Billy Wilder, I. A. L. Diamond” ↗. Crediting an actor with a screenwriter’s sentence is the commonest error in film quotation.
Osgood is the speaker AFI names for the line ↗, and naming him as the speaker is correct. He cannot be its author: characters do not write their dialogue.

Wilder directed, produced and co-wrote, so his name absorbs the film. The screenplay credit is shared with I. A. L. Diamond on AFI’s own listing ↗ and on the Academy Award nomination. The pull toward Wilder alone is strengthened by his epitaph, a paraphrase of the line: “I’m a writer but then nobody’s perfect” ↗ — which is his own joke about the line, not a claim to sole credit.

items.tag: the other half of the scene
items.why: Lemmon is in the shot and is the reason for the joke, but the transcription shows him speaking the set-up ↗ — whipping off the wig and admitting he is a man. The punchline is Osgood’s reply.

items.who: the film, as coiner of the phrase
items.why: The scene is original to the screenplay, but the expression was not invented for it. George Eliot has Caleb Garth say “Well, well, nobody’s perfect, but” in Middlemarch, vol. II (1872) ↗. The film made the words famous; it did not make them up.
Quoted without the opening “Well,” the line loses the beat that makes it a shrug. Both the transcription ↗ and AFI keep the word.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence is accurate as it is usually quoted: AFI lists it at No. 48 as “Well, nobody’s perfect.” ↗ Its authors are Billy Wilder and I. A. L. Diamond. Osgood Fielding III is the character who says it and Joe E. Brown is the actor who says it — neither of them wrote it.

context.heading: The most famous last line in American comedy
lead: Jerry, hiding from the Chicago mob in a dress and calling himself Daphne, has accidentally acquired a fiancé: the wealthy, serenely unbothered Osgood Fielding III. In the boat at the end of the picture, Jerry tries to get out of the engagement by confessing escalating faults — he is not a natural blonde, he smokes, he has a terrible past, he can never have children — and Osgood forgives each one in turn. Out of excuses, Jerry pulls off the wig and drops into his own voice. Osgood barely blinks.

The line was very nearly not the line at all. Wikipedia’s account of the film, citing The Hollywood Reporter ↗, records that Diamond and Wilder put it into the script as a placeholder until they could think of something better, and never did. Whatever was said in the writers’ room, the four words survived the shoot, the release and sixty-odd years of quotation without a syllable changing — which is rarer than it sounds, and is the reason this page ends up confirming the wording rather than correcting it.
context.detailsSummary: Did the film originate the line?
detailsBody: The scene is original to the screenplay; the phrase is not. Some Like It Hot is an adaptation — the story credit goes to Robert Thoeren and Michael Logan for the 1935 French film Fanfare of Love ↗, whose 1951 German remake supplied the working script after the original proved untraceable. But the same source records that Wilder built the gangster plot himself, and the closing beat — Osgood, the boat, the wig — belongs to the Wilder and Diamond screenplay, not to any novel or play. There is no earlier book to hand the credit back to.

The four words, though, were ordinary English long before 1959. George Eliot gives them to Caleb Garth in Middlemarch: “Well, well, nobody’s perfect, but” — page 58 of the 1872 second volume ↗, in a quiet scene between a father and daughter about the compromises of marriage. This is an observation, not a claim of descent: no evidence connects Eliot to Wilder, and nothing here suggests the phrase was rare. What the film did was not coin the words but find the one situation in which they land as a punchline.

sourcesVerified.claim: The film's closing exchange is transcribed as Jerry whipping off his wig and saying "Uhhh, I'm a man!", with Osgood replying "Well, nobody's perfect!" — matching the popular wording.

AFI's 100 Years...100 Movie Quotes lists "Well, nobody's perfect." at No. 48 from Some Like It Hot (1959) and credits "Writer: Billy Wilder, I. A. L. Diamond"; its synopsis names the character Osgood Fielding III.

Screenplay by Billy Wilder and I. A. L. Diamond; story by Robert Thoeren and Michael Logan; based on the 1935 French film Fanfare of Love, with Wilder creating the gangster subplot; studio The Mirisch Company, distributor United Artists, released March 19, 1959; the closing line was put in the script as a placeholder; Osgood replies "Well, nobody's perfect!"
The AFI list entry No. 48 is tabulated with the quote "Well, nobody's perfect.", the character Osgood Fielding III, and the performer Joe E. Brown.

Billy Wilder lived June 22, 1906 – March 27, 2002; in Some Like It Hot, Lemmon reveals he is a man and Brown replies "Well, nobody's perfect"; Wilder's epitaph is "I'm a writer but then nobody's perfect."

I. A. L. Diamond lived June 27, 1920 – April 21, 1988 and was a Romanian-American screenwriter best known for his collaborations with Billy Wilder. (Cited only for these facts; this page does not contain the quote.)
George Eliot's Middlemarch, vol. II (1872), page 58, has Caleb Garth say "Well, well, nobody's perfect, but" — the phrase in print long before the 1959 film.
